excerpt_original: From stage to screen, the exhibition "Stardust: 100 Years of Stage, Screen and Celebrity" traces a century of celebrity portraiture through the work of women photographers. It also inaugurates the new museum and gallery space of Hundred Heroines, a British organisation dedicated…

blocks.text: Hundred Heroines, devoted to promoting and championing women photographers, begins with an observation that has long gone unaddressed: behind the greatest portraits of twentieth-century stars, there was almost always a woman behind the lens. Its ambition is to restore these women to the centre of photographic history — a history they helped write, from which they have too often been erased.

For the earliest works in the show, Hundred Heroines has partnered with Sisters of the Lens, an organisation dedicated to promoting women photographers who worked between the 1850s and 1960s, which has made rare original prints available for this exhibition.

Three unjustly forgotten pioneers are brought back into the light: Lallie Charles, an Irish photographer based in London and one of the most celebrated society portraitists of the Edwardian era: Dorothy Wilding, the first woman appointed as Official Royal Photographer to the British Crown, whose portraits of Elizabeth II appeared on UK postage stamps; and Madame D’Ora, an Austrian photographer who established herself first in Vienna, then in Paris from 1925 onwards, as one of the defining portraitists of fashion and high society in the first half of the twentieth century.

These pioneers immortalized, among others, the British actress Vivien Leigh, whom the world first encountered in Gone with the Wind (1939), the blazing American entertainer Tallulah Bankhead, and the German-American star Marlene Dietrich, the supreme icon of pre-war cinema.

South African photographer Jillian Edelstein, born in Cape Town and based in London since the 1980s, dominates the contemporary section of the exhibition. Trained in photojournalism and published in the New York Times Magazine and Vogue , she pursues in every portrait “the humanity behind the mask of celebrity, the person behind the persona.”

Among Edelstein’s most powerful images is her portrait of the late British punk fashion designer Vivienne Westwood, who died in 2022, shot with her wild flame-orange hair and two small silver horns tucked into her curls, her expression poised somewhere between mischief and majesty. Amy Winehouse, the prodigiously gifted British soul and jazz singer who died at 27 in 2011, appears with arms folded and gaze averted — at once an icon and a raw, exposed soul.

The archive of Elisabeth Buchmeyer-Lewis, a British photographer specializing in the music world of the late twentieth century, provides an electric counterpoint. Her images plunge into the backstage world of British rock and jazz of the 1970s and 1980s: Ian Dury, singer, lyricist and founder of the Blockheads, hunched over his microphone at the legendary 100 Club on Oxford Street, alongside previously unseen photographs of American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan and British hard rock band Led Zeppelin, captured at close range from the stage. Taken together, these portraits measure the full extent of what women photographers gave to pop culture, and to the century that consumed it. “Stardust” puts the record straight.

“Stardust: 100 Years of Stage, Screen and Celebrity” by Hundred Heroines is on view at the new Hundred Heroines Photo Museum in Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, UK, from 11 September to 20 November 2026. Free admission.
